title: Lesson 1.7: Reading signatures and simulating transactions
use: Lesson 1.7 page in the Whop course. Hand-written gold-standard script: simulation, typed-data fields, blind signing and EIP-7702 delegation as walk-throughs, with a dedicated Permit2-phishing worked example.

scenes.title: Reading signatures and simulating transactions
scenes.sub: Know what it does before you approve it.
scenes.vo: Lesson one point seven. Reading signatures and simulating transactions. By the end, you'll know exactly what a signature or transaction will do, before you ever approve it.
scenes.cap: Lesson 1.7. Reading signatures and simulating transactions. By the end, you'll know exactly what a signature or transaction will do, before you ever approve it.

scenes.title: What this lesson covers
scenes.vo: Here's the plan. Simulation, which previews the balance changes before you sign anything. Typed-data signatures, and the four fields worth reading on every single one. Blind signing, and why it should stay off by default. And account delegation, the newest and most powerful thing a signature can now do to your wallet.

stats: if you can't say what it does, don't sign it
scenes.vo: One rule to hold onto through all four topics, before the detail. If you can't say, in one plain sentence, what a prompt actually does, that's not a detail to skip past. It's the answer already: don't sign it.

scenes.title: Preview it before you approve it
scenes.sub: Good wallets show you the outcome first.
scenes.vo: Simulation.

scenes.title: How a simulation preview actually works

nodes.label: Wallet simulates it
nodes.sub: Runs it against current state, without broadcasting

nodes.label: You decide
nodes.sub: With the real result in front of you

scenes.vo: Here's what a good wallet, or a transaction simulator built into one, actually does before you ever sign. You ask for an action, say a swap. Before showing you the signing prompt, it runs that exact transaction against current chain state, without broadcasting it. And it shows you the result in plain terms: balances leaving, and balances arriving. You're not guessing what a contract call does. You're looking at the outcome, in advance.

left.label: What you expected
items: Exactly the asset you intended, leaving
Exactly the asset you intended, arriving
Nothing else moves

right.label: Stop and re-check
items: An asset leaving you never mentioned
An approval appearing you didn't ask for
Your entire balance of something, touched

scenes.vo: So here's the check that actually matters, every time that preview appears. A normal, expected preview shows exactly what you intended, one asset out, one asset in, nothing else moving. A warning sign is a preview showing an asset leaving that you never mentioned, an approval appearing you didn't ask for, or your entire balance of something being touched.

scenes.title: No simulator available? Do this instead
steps: Look up the contract on a block explorer; confirm it's verified
Read the actual function name being called
Start with a small test amount first
scenes.result: A manual check, when a preview isn't there to do it for you
scenes.vo: Not every wallet or every action has a simulator attached, so here's the manual fallback when you don't get a preview. Look up the contract on a block explorer first, and check it's verified. Read the actual function name the transaction calls, not just the button you clicked. And start with a small test amount before ever sending your full position through an unfamiliar contract.

scenes.q: A simulator previews your swap and shows an unrelated token leaving your wallet too. What do you do?
scenes.a: Stop. That's not the transaction you asked for.
scenes.vo: Quick check. A simulator previews your swap and shows an unrelated token leaving your wallet too. What do you do? [[pause 4]] The answer: stop. That's not the transaction you asked for, whatever the interface claims it's doing.

scenes.title: Four fields, read every time
scenes.sub: A structured message, not a random blob of text.
scenes.vo: Typed-data signatures.

lines: with no transaction, and no gas.
scenes.sub: Nothing about the cost warns you. Reading the fields does.
scenes.vo: First, what a typed-data signature actually is, since “Permit” sounds harmless. It's a standard called E.I.P. seven-twelve: a structured message, like an order or a token approval, that your wallet can show you as readable fields instead of raw bytes. A “Permit” or “Permit2” signature specifically can hand over token access without any transaction, and without any gas. That's exactly why it's worth reading carefully; nothing about the cost warns you.

scenes.title: The four fields, every time

nodes.label: Spender
nodes.sub: Which address, and do you recognise it

nodes.label: Deadline
nodes.sub: How long the grant stays valid

scenes.vo: Here are the four fields that matter on every single typed-data prompt, in the order to actually read them. Spender: which address is being given access, and do you recognise it. Token: which asset this covers. Amount: a specific number, or “unlimited.” And deadline: how long this grant stays valid, sometimes years away. Read all four, every time, before you sign anything.

scenes.title: Turning the four fields into a decision
steps: Unfamiliar spender? That alone is reason to stop
Amount: matches this action, or unlimited?
Deadline: does it really need years of validity?
scenes.result: Most bad Permits get caught right here
scenes.vo: Put those four fields into a decision you can actually make in the moment. Read the spender first, and if it's unfamiliar, that alone is reason to stop. Check whether the amount matches what this one action needs, or reads as unlimited. Check the deadline: real actions rarely need years of validity. And if any of the three feels wrong, reject and re-check, rather than assume the interface knows best.

left.label: A classic approval
items: Its own on-chain transaction
Costs gas; you'd notice it as a step

right.label: A Permit / Permit2 signature
items: Off-chain, free, and instant
Bundled invisibly into your action

scenes.vo: Worth knowing why “Permit” signatures exist at all, since it's a real convenience, not just a risk. A classic approval is its own on-chain transaction: it costs gas, and you'd notice it as a separate step. A Permit or Permit2 signature does the same job, off-chain and free, bundled invisibly into the action you were already taking. Convenient when you understand it. Exactly why it also needs reading.

scenes.q: What can a “Permit” signature grant, without any transaction or gas at all?
scenes.a: Token access, for the spender, amount and duration in the message.
scenes.vo: Quick check. What can a “Permit” signature grant, without any transaction or gas at all? [[pause 4]] The answer: token access, for the spender, amount and duration written into the message, exactly as shown in those four fields.

scenes.title: When your wallet can't show you what you're signing
scenes.sub: And the newest, most powerful signature of all.
scenes.vo: Blind signing, and delegation.

left.label: Normal signing
items: Device decodes the transaction
Shows readable fields: spender, amount, deadline

right.label: Blind signing
items: Device can't decode it
Shows only a hash — tells you nothing

scenes.vo: Here's the distinction that matters on a hardware wallet specifically. Normal signing decodes the transaction and shows you readable fields, spender, amount, deadline, the works. Blind signing is what happens when the device can't decode it: you see only a hash, a string of characters that tells you nothing about what you're actually approving.

scenes.title: The blind-signing habit
steps: On only for one verified, understood action
scenes.result: A hash tells you nothing — don't sign what you can't read
scenes.vo: So here's the actual rule for blind signing, as a habit. Keep it off by default, every day, on every device. Turn it on only for one specific, already-verified action you understand. Complete that one action. Then turn it straight back off, before you forget you left it on.

scenes.title: What an account-delegation signature actually does

nodes.label: Behaviour delegated
nodes.sub: To smart-contract code you may not have read

nodes.label: Malicious code = full control
nodes.sub: The attacker's contract now runs your account

scenes.vo: Now the newest risk: account delegation, under a standard called E.I.P. seventy-seven-oh-two, live since Ethereum's twenty twenty-five Pectra upgrade. Normally, a wallet is just a key. This lets that same wallet sign an authorisation that delegates its behaviour to smart-contract code instead. A legitimate app might use this for useful features. A malicious site can use the exact same signature to hand your entire account over to an attacker.

scenes.title: What happens after a malicious delegation

nodes.label: No undo
nodes.sub: Nothing to call, nothing to reverse

scenes.vo: And here's what actually happens next, once a malicious delegation signature goes through. The attacker's contract is now the code controlling your account, immediately. It can move every asset the account holds, without asking for a single further signature from you. This often happens within minutes of the signing, sometimes faster. And once it's done, it's done: there's no undo, and no support line to call.

scenes.kicker: The narrowest rule in this lesson
lines: for a purpose you can state in one sentence.
scenes.sub: An unfamiliar site asking for this wants control of the whole account.
scenes.vo: So the rule for delegation signatures is narrower than for anything else in this lesson, on purpose. Only sign one from a wallet feature or app you already trust, for a purpose you can state in one sentence. An unfamiliar site asking for a delegation isn't offering you a feature. It's asking for control of the whole account, in a single signature.

left.label: A legitimate delegation
items: A feature you deliberately chose
From an app you already trust

right.label: A malicious delegation request
items: An unfamiliar site, out of nowhere
No purpose you could state in a sentence

scenes.vo: Delegation itself isn't automatically the enemy here, so here's the honest contrast. A legitimate use is a wallet feature you deliberately chose, upgrading your own account to add multisig or spending limits, from an app you already trust. A malicious one is an unfamiliar site asking for the exact same signature, with no feature explained, no purpose you could state back in a sentence.

scenes.q: Your hardware wallet shows only a hash for a transaction, no readable fields. What should your default response be?
scenes.a: Don't sign it. Keep blind signing off by default.
scenes.vo: Quick check. Your hardware wallet shows only a hash for a transaction, no readable fields. What should your default response be? [[pause 4]] The answer: don't sign it. Keep blind signing off, and only enable it briefly for one action you already understand.

scenes.title: “Verify your wallet”, one field at a time
scenes.sub: Reading the four fields turns a scam into an obvious one.
scenes.vo: Worked example.

A site asks you to “verify your wallet.” Your wallet shows a typed-data message: Permit2, token U.S.D.C., spender zero x nine f three a, dot dot dot, c three, amount one one five, seven nine two, oh eight nine and more, which is the unlimited number, deadline twenty thirty. Read those four fields and the trick collapses instantly. This isn't verification. It's unlimited U.S.D.C. access, for a spender you've never seen, for the next five years.
scenes.cap: A site asks you to “verify your wallet.” Your wallet shows a typed-data message: Permit2, token USDC, spender 0x9f3a…c3, amount 115792089… (the unlimited number), deadline 2030. Read those four fields and the trick collapses instantly. This isn't verification. It's unlimited USDC access, for a spender you've never seen, for the next five years.

stats: drained per wallet in documented Permit2 phishing cases (outside research)
scenes.vo: One real, dated fact behind why this exact scam works so well. Security researchers have documented Permit and Permit2 phishing signatures draining six- and seven-figure sums from individual wallets in a single approval, across 2023 and 2024. Not a rare edge case: one of the highest-value theft techniques currently in use, and it starts with exactly the prompt you just read.

scenes.title: What you actually do with this prompt
scenes.result: No real verification ever needs a token approval
scenes.vo: So here's exactly what you do with that prompt in front of you, right now. Reject the signature, don't sign it under any circumstance. Close the tab completely; don't navigate elsewhere on that same site. And go check your existing approvals afterward, since a site willing to try this once may have others live from before you knew to look.

scenes.title: Checking your existing approvals, step by step
scenes.vo: And here's what “check your existing approvals” actually means as a walk-through, since it's worth doing on a schedule, not just after a scare. Open an approval-checker tool for your wallet address. Review the full list of spenders it shows you, not just the newest one. Revoke anything unfamiliar, or anything unlimited you no longer need. And put a reminder in your calendar to repeat this, since old approvals accumulate quietly.

scenes.title: Your checklist
steps: Simulated balance changes shown before signing
Spender, token, amount, deadline: read every time
Delegations only from apps you already trust
scenes.vo: Here's your checklist. Do it now, for real. Your wallet shows simulated balance changes before you sign, every time. You read spender, token, amount and deadline on every typed-data prompt. Blind signing stays off on your hardware wallet by default. And you never sign an account-delegation request from a site or app you don't already trust.

scenes.title: Recap
items: Simulation: preview the outcome before you commit
Typed-data: four fields, read every time
Blind signing: hides those fields, so it stays off by default
Delegation: the newest, most powerful signature — narrowest trust rule
scenes.vo: Let's recap. Four ideas, one shared habit underneath them. Simulation previews the outcome before you commit to it. Typed-data signatures reduce to four fields worth reading, every time. Blind signing hides those fields, so it stays off unless you've verified the action yourself. And account delegation is the newest, most powerful signature of all, worth the narrowest trust rule you have.
Read every prompt, and simulate before you sign, and the vast majority of what could go wrong on-chain simply stops reaching you. Next up, Lesson one point eight: Privacy and physical security.
